preamble: Pharyngealization (emphaticization) of plain [s] to the emphatic [sˤ], Arabic ṣād ص. The documented cases are loanwords in Arabic, in which Italian, French and English s is taken over as ṣ in words such as these: Italian sala > صالة, French salon > صالون /sˤaː.luːn/, English bus > باص [bɑːsˤ]. The adaptation is not uniform: Egyptian 'elevator', from French ascenseur, is given both as أسانسير with plain /ʔa.san.seːr/ and as أصانصير with emphatic /ʔa.sˤan.sˤeːr/. Ottoman Turkish also borrowed salon and salsa, so an Ottoman intermediary cannot be ruled out for those two, although Wiktionary gives the Arabic words as borrowed directly from French and Italian. Wiktionary gives صِرَاط ṣirāṭ 'path' as a variant of سِرَاط sirāṭ, borrowed from Syriac ˀesṭrāṭ (itself from Latin strāta), so that older loan has both s and ṣ. Arabic قَصْر qaṣr 'castle' is not counted: its ṣ was already in the Aramaic source qaṣrā (Wiktionary). The reverse change, loss of emphasis in Maltese and Cypriot Arabic, is filed under [sˤ] > [s].

examples.to: Arabic صالة 'hall, large room', South Levantine ṣāle [ˈsˤɑː.le]

examples.note: Both s become ṣ. Ottoman Turkish had صالسه (salsa), a direct borrowing from Italian, now obsolete, beside صالچه (salça) via Greek (Wiktionary salça).

examples.to: Arabic صالون /sˤaː.luːn/ 'reception hall, salon', Moroccan ṣālūn 'living room'
examples.note: Ottoman Turkish صالون was also borrowed from French (same Wiktionary page).

examples.to: Egyptian أصانصير ʔaṣanṣēr /ʔa.sˤan.sˤeːr/, also أسانسير ʔasansēr /ʔa.san.seːr/ 'elevator'
examples.note: Wiktionary gives the emphatic spelling as an alternative form.

examples.to: Arabic باص bāṣ 'bus', Gulf (Kuwait) /bɑːsˤ/, South Levantine [bɑːsˤ]

examples.note: Wiktionary gives both English and French soda as the source.
